title: What Does Ephesians Say About Speech? The Words You Thought Were Small May Be Revealing Who Is Ruling Your Heart
paragraphs: What Does Ephesians Say About Speech? The Words You Thought Were Small May Be Revealing Who Is Ruling Your Heart
Paul does not merely tell Christians to stop saying bad things. He shows us what happens when a mouth that once wounded people comes under the transforming grace of Jesus Christ.
There are wounds on your body that eventually disappear.
Then there are sentences you can still hear twenty years later.
“You’ll never amount to anything.”
“I wish I never married you.”
“You’re just like your father.”
“I’m done with you.”
“Nobody wants you here.”
Sometimes the person who said it forgot before the day was over.
But the person who heard it carried it for decades.
That is the terrifying power of speech.
And perhaps that is why one of the most piercing passages about Christian speech was not written as a collection of etiquette rules.
It was written in the middle of Paul’s description of what happens when Jesus Christ gives someone a new life.
Ephesians does not ask merely, “Do Christians swear?”
It asks something much more uncomfortable.
What kind of person is speaking through your mouth?
Because you can sing worship songs on Sunday and destroy someone with your words on Monday.
You can know Bible verses and still know exactly which sentence will hurt your spouse the deepest.
You can post Scripture publicly and assassinate someone privately.
You can say, “I’m just being honest,” when honesty has become camouflage for cruelty.
You can avoid profanity and still gossip.
You can speak politely and still manipulate.
You can tell the truth in such a vicious way that you secretly enjoy watching it wound.
And Ephesians will not allow us to hide behind the excuse that words are “just words.”
Paul begins somewhere deeper.
Before he addresses the mouth, he addresses the person.

He tells believers that they have learned Christ differently from the world around them. The old self is to be put away, the mind is to be renewed, and the new self is to be put on, a life shaped according to God in righteousness and holiness (Ephesians 4:20–24).
Then comes the speech.
The connection matters.
Christian speech is not behavior modification pasted onto an unchanged heart.
It is supposed to be evidence of a changed person.
Paul writes in Ephesians 4:25:
apothemenoi to pseudos, laleite alētheian.
The sense is straightforward:
Having put away falsehood, speak truth.
Notice that Paul does not merely say, “Try lying less.”
Falsehood belongs to something being discarded.
Truth belongs to the new life.
And Paul gives a remarkable reason: believers are members of one another.
That changes everything.
Lying to another member of Christ’s body is not merely breaking an abstract rule. It damages a relationship God designed for unity.
Imagine your left hand deliberately deceiving your right hand.
Absurd.
Self-destructive.
Yet Paul says, in effect, that this is what falsehood does inside the body of Christ.
So the Christian asks more than, “Is what I am about to say technically true?”
We ask:
Is it truthful?
Is it necessary?
What is motivating me?
Am I trying to restore someone or embarrass them?
Am I exposing sin because I love righteousness—or exposing a sinner because I enjoy the scandal?
That last question should make some of us uncomfortable.
Because Christians can become fascinated with scandal while claiming to defend holiness.
We can share someone’s failure faster than we share someone’s testimony of restoration.
We can screenshot weakness.
Forward rumors.
Repackage gossip as a “prayer request.”
Write comments about people we have never met.
Destroy reputations with information we never verified.
And then reassure ourselves that we never technically lied.
But Paul keeps going.
Ephesians 4:29 contains one of the strongest descriptions of speech in the New Testament:
“πᾶς λόγος σαπρὸς ἐκ τοῦ στόματος ὑμῶν μὴ ἐκπορευέσθω”
pas logos sapros ek tou stomatos hymōn mē ekporeuesthō.
The idea is:
Let no corrupt or rotten word proceed from your mouth.
The word that should stop us is σαπρός — sapros.
Rotten.
Bad.
Unfit.
Worthless.
The word is used elsewhere in the New Testament for things such as bad fruit. Here Paul applies that imagery to speech.
Think about that.
Some words are rotten before they ever leave the mouth.
And rotten things spread decay.
You know this already because you have probably watched one sentence change the temperature of an entire room.
A husband walks through the door exhausted.
His wife says something sharp.
He fires something sharper back.
A child hears it.
Someone brings up something that happened three years ago.
Another wound gets reopened.
Voices rise.
Doors close.
Nobody remembers exactly how the argument started.
But everybody feels what the words created.
Or maybe your battlefield is not a kitchen.
Maybe it is Facebook.
You see a post.
Your blood pressure rises.
Your fingers move faster than your wisdom.
You type the comment.
You reread it.
Something inside whispers, Don’t.
But anger answers, They deserve it.
So you press Post.
For a few seconds it feels powerful.
Then the Holy Spirit begins pressing somewhere much deeper than the screen.
Because the question was never merely whether you could win the argument.
The question was whether Christ could be seen in the way you spoke.
Paul does not stop at prohibition.
This is where Ephesians becomes breathtaking.
He does not simply tell us what must not leave the mouth.
He tells us what should.
The rest of Ephesians 4:29 says our speech should be good for οἰκοδομήν — oikodomēn, building up, according to the need, so that it may “δῷ χάριν τοῖς ἀκούουσιν” — dō charin tois akouousin:
give grace to those who hear.
Read that slowly.
Give grace to those who hear.
Your mouth can become an instrument through which another human being receives grace.
Not saving grace originating from you—only Christ saves.
But speech shaped by His grace can strengthen, encourage, correct, comfort, restore, and build another person.
That means before words leave your mouth, a profoundly Christian question can govern them:
What does this person need from me right now that would honor Christ?
Sometimes the answer is encouragement.
Sometimes silence.
Sometimes an apology.
Sometimes a warning.
Sometimes correction.
Sometimes the truth nobody else has been willing to say.
Biblical speech is not perpetual niceness.
Jesus Himself spoke hard truth.
Paul spoke hard truth.
Truth can confront.
Love can rebuke.
Grace does not require pretending sin is harmless.
Ephesians itself commands believers to speak truth.
But there is a difference between truth used as medicine and truth used as a weapon.
A surgeon cuts to heal.
An attacker cuts to harm.
The instrument may penetrate in both cases.
The intention and outcome are radically different.
So perhaps the question is not merely, “Was I right?”
Maybe tonight the question is:
Why did I enjoy saying it?
That question reaches places religious appearances cannot.
Why did their embarrassment satisfy you?
Why did you need everybody to know what they did?
Why did you tell that story again?
Why did you make that sarcastic comment?
Why do you speak to strangers more kindly than you speak to the person who sleeps beside you?
Why does everyone at church receive your patience while your children receive whatever anger is left when you come home?
Why can you worship Jesus with your mouth and then use that same mouth to humiliate someone made in His image?
Paul moves immediately from speech to something astonishing:
“καὶ μὴ λυπεῖτε τὸ πνεῦμα τὸ ἅγιον τοῦ θεοῦ”
And do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God.
That is Ephesians 4:30.
The placement is sobering.
Paul has spoken about corrupt speech, and then he speaks about grieving the Holy Spirit. The surrounding passage continues with bitterness, wrath, anger, clamor, slander and malice being put away.
Our words are not spiritually insignificant.
The Holy Spirit is not an impersonal religious force.
Paul speaks of Him personally: He can be grieved.
Think about the argument you had.
Think about the message you sent.
Think about the gossip you repeated.
Think about the person you publicly mocked.
Think about the child whose confidence you crushed because you were angry.
Think about the spouse you punished with sentences designed to reopen old wounds.
There was another Presence in that room.
And suddenly this is no longer merely about communication skills.
It is about communion with God.
But if conviction is beginning to rise inside you, do not run from this article yet.
Because Ephesians does not end the story with your failure.
Thank God.
It does not end with the screenshot.
It does not end with the screaming match.
It does not end with the sentence you desperately wish you could pull back into your mouth.
It does not end with your worst moment.
Paul continues:
Put away bitterness.
Put away wrath.
Put away anger.
Put away clamor.
Put away slander.
Put away malice.
Then Ephesians 4:32 turns toward something beautiful:
Be kind.
Be tenderhearted.
Forgive one another.
And then Paul gives the foundation that makes all of this Christian rather than merely therapeutic:
God has forgiven you in Christ.
There it is.
Jesus.
Not “be nicer so God will finally accept you.”
Not “clean up your vocabulary so you can earn heaven.”
Not “become respectable enough to deserve grace.”
The Gospel moves in the opposite direction.
God's forgiveness in Christ becomes the pattern and power for how forgiven people treat other people.
You were guilty.
Christ came.
You could not rescue yourself.
Christ bore sin and conquered death.
You brought Him nothing with which to purchase forgiveness.
Grace met you empty-handed.
And when a person begins to understand how much he has been forgiven, something happens to the way he speaks about the failures of others.
The Cross destroys superiority.
You cannot stand beneath a crucified Savior bragging about how much better you are than the sinner beside you.
At Calvary, boasting dies.
At Calvary, masks fall.
At Calvary, scandal meets grace.
And maybe your scandal was your mouth.
Maybe nobody knows.
Maybe everyone thinks you are gentle.
But your family knows another version.
Maybe your scandal is gossip.
Maybe sarcasm.
Maybe uncontrolled anger.
Maybe lying.
Maybe flattery.
Maybe online cruelty.
Maybe passive-aggressive silence.
Maybe you learned to weaponize Bible verses so effectively that you can hurt someone and make it sound spiritual.
Jesus is not asking you to hide it better.
He is calling you to repentance.
And repentance is not merely feeling terrible about yourself.
Biblical repentance turns.
It brings the sin into the light.
It agrees with God.
It stops defending what Christ died to redeem us from.
Maybe your next act of worship is not another worship song.
Maybe it is walking into the other room and saying:
I was wrong.
What I said was sinful.
You did not deserve to be spoken to that way.
Please forgive me.
No “but you made me angry.”
No “if you were offended.”
No carefully constructed apology that secretly puts the blame back on the wounded person.
Just truth.
Humility.
Repentance.
Grace.
And perhaps the hardest words you will ever speak are the words that finally begin healing your home.
Ephesians also reaches beyond obvious verbal cruelty.
Paul later warns in Ephesians 5:4 about obscene, foolish, and crude speech, contrasting these with thanksgiving.
Again, notice the replacement.
Christianity does not merely empty the mouth.
Christ fills it differently.
Falsehood gives way to truth.
Rotten speech gives way to words that build.
Bitterness and slander give way to kindness and forgiveness.
Corrupt joking gives way to thanksgiving.
The Gospel does not simply put a muzzle on the old person.
Jesus makes a new person.
That is the deeper answer to the question, “What does Ephesians say about speech?”
Ephesians says your words should increasingly sound like they belong to someone who has been forgiven.
Someone who has been loved.
Someone who has been rescued.
Someone who belongs to Christ.
Someone whose identity is no longer anchored in winning arguments, controlling people, humiliating enemies, protecting ego, spreading rumors, or proving superiority.
And this means there is hope even if your words have done terrible damage.
Consequences may remain.
Trust may require time to rebuild.
Some words cannot simply be forgotten because you apologized.
Repentance does not demand that wounded people instantly pretend nothing happened.
But Jesus Christ specializes in resurrection.
He restores sinners.
He changes hearts.
He teaches angry mouths another language.
He turns liars into truth-tellers.
He turns gossipers into protectors.
He turns accusers into intercessors.
He turns people who once tore others down into people who build them up.
He can teach the mouth that once released poison to release grace.
That is not self-improvement.
That is transformation.
And maybe someone reading this is thinking about one particular person right now.
You know exactly who.
A name appeared in your mind several paragraphs ago.
Call them.
Message them.
Go to them if appropriate.
Own what you did.
Do not wait for them to apologize first.
Your obedience to Christ is not conditional upon somebody else's repentance.
And if you are the wounded person—the one still carrying somebody else's sentence—remember this too:
What they called you is not necessarily what God calls you.
Their cruelty is not your identity.
Their rejection is not your final verdict.
Your worth is not decided by the angriest person who ever spoke over you.
Look to Christ.
If you belong to Him, your deepest identity is found in the One who redeemed you.
Maybe somebody called you worthless.
Jesus considered sinners worth pursuing at immeasurable cost.
Maybe somebody called you hopeless.
Jesus walked out of a grave.
Maybe somebody knows your scandal and believes your story is over.
They have underestimated grace.
From scandal to grace is not a slogan when Jesus Christ gets involved. It is what redemption does.
Jesus rewrites people.
And rewritten people begin speaking differently.
Before you speak today, remember three realities without turning them into another religious checklist:
There is a person in front of you.
There is a God who hears you.
And there is a Gospel you represent.
So speak truth.
Speak what builds.
Speak what fits the genuine need.
Speak grace.
And when you fail, repent quickly.
Do not protect your pride while your relationships bleed.
Run to Christ.
Receive again the wonder of His mercy.
Then go make things right where you can.
Be honest.
And if Jesus has already transformed the way you speak, tell part of that testimony. Somebody scrolling through the comments may need evidence that Christ is still changing people.
Not because clicking “Share” earns favor with God. It does not.
It cannot.
Christ alone saves, entirely by grace.
But if this biblical message helped you, sharing it can become a simple act of witness and service.

Supporting Gospel ministry is not a way to buy God's favor, prove that you glorify God, or earn spiritual status. The Gospel will never be for sale. But generous, willing support can genuinely glorify God when it flows from gratitude, love, and a desire to help biblical truth reach more people. Scripture calls Christian giving willing rather than coerced, so this invitation is exactly that: an invitation.

If you have been reading quietly for months, perhaps this is your opportunity to move from consuming the mission to helping carry it—not because God needs your money, and never because salvation can be purchased, but because Gospel-centered work is worth supporting when God has given you both the desire and ability to do so.
Let the sentence somebody encounters today be different from the sentence that wounded you years ago.
Let truth travel farther than gossip.
Let grace travel farther than scandal.
Let the words attached to your name increasingly make people thirsty for the Christ whose name you carry.
Because someday, many of the arguments we thought we had to win will be forgotten.
The comments will disappear.
The posts will sink beneath thousands of newer posts.
The applause will fade.
But the people we loved—or wounded—with our words will remember how it felt to stand near us.
So before the next sentence leaves your mouth, remember:
A heart captured by grace should not be comfortable making another soul bleed with words.
And when you realize yours still does sometimes, do not hide from Jesus.
Run to Him.
Repent.
Receive mercy.
Get up.
Go apologize.
And let the Savior who rewrote your eternity begin rewriting your vocabulary.
Your mouth may carry the evidence of yesterday's scandal, but surrendered to Jesus, it can become an instrument of tomorrow's grace.
